newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Moment of truth for Zaire's Mobutu, rebels advance.
newsitem.headline: Moment of truth for Zaire's Mobutu, rebels advance.

text.p: Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko, battling cancer and a whirlwind revolt at home, meets his civil war foe Laurent Kabila on Sunday for peace talks aboard a converted icebreaker.

South African officials told reporters on the SAS Outeniqua that Mobutu, one of a vanishing breed of veteran African strongmen, would join Kabila and South Africa's Nelson Mandela on the South African naval vessel for talks on Sunday morning.

With Kabila's forces closing in on the capital Kinshasa, The New York Times reported in its Sunday edition that Mobutu had written to U.S. President Bill Clinton telling him that he was prepared to stand down after more than three decades in power.
"The decision for him to leave has been made," a senior American official is quoted as saying.
The major issue holding up the resignation appeared to be whether Kabila would seize undivided power or share it with other political forces, the newspaper reported.
South African officials on the Russian-built Outeniqua, which was moored in Congo's port of Pointe Noire, said that Mandela had an assurance from Mobutu that he would attend.

"Mr Kabila is here now and the meeting will start some time tomorrow and we hope they will begin to solve their problems," South African Deputy Foreign Minister Aziz Pahad told reporters late on Saturday.
Kabila, whose forces took up arms in October and control three quarters of the sprawling nation at the heart of Africa, boarded the ship by helicopter late on Saturday.
One diplomat said that the rebel leader was looking for any excuse not to come. At one point, a frustrated Mandela got on the satellite phone to him and shouted down the line.
Mobutu, 66, seized power in 1965 and was backed during the Cold War by the United States as a bulwark against Soviet communism. He has seen his hold over Zaire broken by Kabila's lightning advances.

Zaire accuses Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi of fighting alongside Kabila's forces. Independent sources say rebel forces have just captured Mobutu's Lisala birthplace and are marching on Kinshasa and his jungle palace in Gbadolite in the north.
The rebels say they are within 150 km (95 miles) of Kinshasa and are moving up reinforcements and heavy weaponry for a final assault on the city of five million people.
The military governor of the teeming capital asked residents to stay calm in the face of the rebel advance and told security forces to protect its population without discrimination.
The U.S. State Department urged American citizens to leave Zaire and warned them not to travel there citing the "deteriorating security and political situation".
Previously Kabila had refused to hold talks in Congo, saying its president, Pascal Lissouba, was too close to Mobutu. He had also said he did not want the talks to start before Sunday.
Officials did not say whether the ship would head for international waters as initially planned before talks began.
Mobutu spent Saturday on shore in Pointe Noire after sailing into international waters with Mandela on Friday for a rendezvous Kabila failed to keep, citing security reasons.
Mobutu boarded the ship with great difficulty on Friday. Unable to climb 31 steep steps, he was driven on board five hours late up a makeshift ramp.
South African officials said security on the Outeniqua had been tightened.
Mobutu aides say talks will focus on a peaceful transition with elections open to all. They reject suggestions that the meeting is a face-saver to allow him to stand down with dignity.
Kabila, 56, says Mobutu must go and has refused to declare a truce for the talks.
The United States, France, former colonial power Belgium and Britain have troops across the Zaire River in Congo to evacuate their nationals from Kinshasa if need be.
